explanations.explanation: Love is the one debt Paul, the apostle, says to keep on the books. Everything else gets paid off, but this one stays open between believers. I think that's the only bill you'd ever want to see show up again next month. Paul says to be indebted to no one, except to one another in love.

Nice thought, friend, and I love a gift as much as the next stamper. But Paul doesn't say gifts here. He says to be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. This debt isn't wrapped in a bow, and you can't return it with the receipt.

Favors feel close, because we all keep a little mental tally of who owes who. Paul doesn't go that way, though. He says to be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. No tally sheet needed for this one, friend.
That's right, and Paul says it plainly: "For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law." Not part of the law, not the easy half. The law. I'd sign up for a deal like that all day long.
Paul actually says the opposite of that. He says, "For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law." So loving your neighbor isn't a side dish to the law. It's the law fulfilled, friend.

That's the one! Paul says the commandments, "and any other commandments, are summed up in this one decree: 'Love your neighbor as yourself.'" That's a whole list squeezed into one sentence. I can't even fit my grocery list on one sticky note, friend.

That's a real commandment, and it's in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:12). But it's not the decree Paul names here. He says all the commandments, and any others, are summed up in this one: "Love your neighbor as yourself." So honoring your father and mother is covered under that big umbrella, too.

That's a real commandment too, and it's found in Exodus 20:8. It's not the one Paul picks as the summary, though. He says, "Love your neighbor as yourself." That's the decree where every other commandment gets folded in.

Paul says it straight: "Love does no wrong to its neighbor." Then he adds, "Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law." Love isn't out there looking for ways to hurt anybody. I wish my first batch of cookies had that kind of track record.

Paul says the reverse. He writes, "Love does no wrong to its neighbor." That's exactly why he can say love is the fulfillment of the law. Love and hurting your neighbor just don't go together, friend.

Slumber is the word. Paul says, "The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber." Notice he says the hour has come. It's not 'whenever you get around to it.' I've been through the sleeping part, friend, and waking up is better.

I see why that one tempts you, since it's a heavy-sounding word. Paul doesn't say sorrow, though. He says, "The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber." He's talking about sleeping, not weeping.

Funny thing, friend, labor would almost be the opposite. Paul isn't telling them to stop working. He says, "The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber." So this is a wake-up call, not a day off from the oven.
Yes, friend. Paul says, "our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed." Every day gets them closer. That's the reason to be wide awake, and it's good news, not a scary one.
A harvest would be a fine thing to have nearby. But Paul doesn't mention one here. He says, "our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed." Salvation is what's drawing closer.

Passover is a real feast, but Paul isn't talking about it in this passage. What he says is, "our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed." That's the thing getting closer, and it's why he wants them awake.

Light it is. Paul says, "let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light." Notice he says "us," so he's in this with them. You take off the dark stuff and you suit up in the light.

Faith is a good word, friend, and I can see why you reached for it. But Paul's words here are, "let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light." He sets light against darkness. That's the pair in this verse.

Truth is a strong word, and I like it. It just isn't the one Paul uses in this verse. He says, "let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light." Darkness goes out, and light goes on.

That's right. Paul says to behave decently, "not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy." So dissension and jealousy sit right on the same list. Tells you he takes a grumbling heart as seriously as a wild night, friend.

Look again, because Paul actually does put them together. He says to behave decently, "not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy." It's all one list. Dissension and jealousy are right there with the rest.

That's the one! Paul says, "Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ." It's the best outfit there is, friend, and it's never going out of style. Better than any fancy hat I've ever worn, and I've worn a tall one.
The prophets mattered a great deal, but Paul doesn't point to them here. He says, "clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ." That's the One they're meant to put on.

Angels are impressive, friend. I've met one, and the light alone will straighten your mustache. But Paul doesn't tell them to clothe themselves with angels. He says, "clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ."
Close the door on that one, friend. Paul says the opposite: "make no provision for the desires of the flesh." He doesn't say to save a little room or keep a backup. It's no provision at all.

Right, there's no 'just in case' in this verse. Paul says, "clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh." It's all in with Jesus, with no room set aside for the other stuff. And that's the last word of the passage.
